Period schedule:

Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: From Repeated Addition to Fraction Times Whole

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 8.1 p.176
textbook_items_in_class.description: A farmer distributes 2/3 acre of land to each of her 5 grandchildren. Total land given = 5 × 2/3 = 10/3 acres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 2, section 8.1 p.176
textbook_items_in_class.description: 1¼ hours of internet time costs ₹8 per hour. Convert 1¼ to 5/4, then 5/4 × 8 = 10. Cost = ₹10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 8.1 p.176
textbook_items_in_class.description: Contextual whole-number × fraction problems: (Q1) Tenzin drinks 1/2 glass of milk daily — glasses in a week and in January; (Q2) workers make 1 km of canal in 8 days — km in 1 day and in 5-day week; (Q3) Manju and 2 neighbours share 5 litres of oil among 3 families — oil per family per week and in 4 weeks; (Q4) Moon sets 5/6 hour later each day — hours after 10 pm on Thursday.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 8.1 p.177
homework.description: Multiply and convert to mixed fractions: (a) 7 × 3/5; (b) 4 × 1/3; (c) 9 × 6/7; (d) 13 × 6/11.

time_bands.activity: Open with whole-number multiplication as repeated addition: ask students how they would compute 3 × 5 by adding 5 three times, then pose the question — what does 3 × 2/3 mean? Draw a number-line on the board and mark jumps of 2/3 to show 3 equal hops, landing on 2.

Walk through Example 1, section 8.1 p.176 ("A farmer distributes 2/3 acre of land to each of her 5 grandchildren....") using the two-step procedure: divide 2 by 3, then multiply by 5 to reach 10/3. Show the number-line model alongside the arithmetic. Follow immediately with Example 2, section 8.1 p.176 ("1¼ hours of internet time costs ₹8 per hour...."), converting 1¼ to 5/4 and applying the same procedure.

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 8.1 p.176 ("Contextual whole-number × fraction problems...."). Circulate and prompt pairs who write only the answer to also show the repeated-addition or two-step route.

Draw pairs out to share one solution each for Q1 and Q4. Record the two-step procedure on the board as a class-generated summary: (i) divide the numerator's whole by the denominator; (ii) multiply by the numerator.

periods.teacher_notes: The number-line distance model (Aaron's walking pace from the section prose) is the conceptual anchor here — students who jump to the formula without the model often misplace the denominator in multi-step contexts. Watch for students who multiply numerator and denominator both by the whole number: the two-step procedure should make clear that only the numerator is multiplied. Figure it Out Q5, section 8.1 p.177 ("Multiply and convert to mixed fractions....") is set as a written exercise to consolidate the procedure.
materials: Ruler or metre stick for number-line demonstration
Printed copies of section 8.1 p.176 problems or textbook

periods.activity_title: Fraction Times Fraction: The Unit-Square Area Model

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.180
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the following products using a unit square as the whole: (a) 1/3 × 1/5; (b) 1/4 × 1/3; (c) 1/5 × 1/2; (d) 1/6 × 1/5. Then find 1/12 × 1/18 without drawing.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 8.1 p.179
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the unit-square model to multiply 5/4 × 3/2. The multiplicand 3/2 is greater than 1; divide it into 4 equal parts to find 3/8, then multiply by 5 to get 15/8.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.181
homework.description: Find the following products using a unit square: (a) 2/3 × 4/5; (b) 1/4 × 2/3; (c) 3/5 × 1/2; (d) 4/6 × 3/5.

time_bands.activity: Draw a large unit square on the board. Ask: if the whole square is 1, how would you shade 2/5 of it? Shade 2 of 5 vertical strips. Now ask: what is 3/4 of that shaded region? Guide students to subdivide the 2 shaded strips into 4 horizontal rows, shade 3 of those rows, and count: 6 out of 20 small rectangles — so 3/4 × 2/5 = 6/20. Record this as area = product of sides.

Link the area model to the general formula a/b × c/d = (a×c)/(b×d), attributing it to Brahmagupta's Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) as the section describes. Introduce cancellation of common factors before multiplying (apavartana), attributing it to Jaina scholar Umasvati (c. 150 CE), with a quick numerical example on the board.

Students individually draw unit-square sketches and compute Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.180 ("Find the following products using a unit square as the whole...."). Encourage them to attempt 1/12 × 1/18 without drawing, using the formula.

Whole-class discussion of Math Talk, section 8.1 p.179 ("Use the unit-square model to multiply 5/4 × 3/2....") — the multiplicand exceeds 1. Ask students how the unit square must be extended; develop the idea that 3/2 means one whole plus 1/2, so the square is extended beyond the unit. Confirm commutativity by rotating the rectangle.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse fraction × fraction with fraction + fraction, applying the addition algorithm (finding a common denominator) by habit. The unit-square model makes the multiplicative structure visual: the product is an area, not a combined length. The historical note on Brahmagupta and Umasvati is a brief, purposeful pause — keep it conversational, not a lecture. Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.181 ("Find the following products using a unit square....") is assigned for written practice.
materials: Graph paper or squared dot paper (one sheet per student)

periods.activity_title: Applying Fraction Multiplication: Contexts and Comparisons

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.183
textbook_items_in_class.description: A tap fills 7/10 of a tank in 1 hour. Find the fraction filled if the tap runs for: (a) 1/3 hour; (b) 2/3 hour; (c) 3/4 hour; (d) 7/10 hour; (e) how long must the tap run to fill the tank completely?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3–Q5, section 8.1 p.183–184
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of a rectangle with sides 3¾ ft and 9⅗ ft (Q3). Tsewang plants 4 saplings with 3/4 m spacing — find first-to-last distance (Q4). Compare 12/15 of 500 g and 3/20 of 4 kg (Q5).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (product comparison), section 8.1 p.185
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore when the product of two numbers is greater than both, between the two, or less than both. Classify into situations based on whether each factor is between 0 and 1 or greater than 1, fill in the table with examples, and complete the blanks about the relationship.

homework.description: The government takes 1/6 of Somu's land for a road. She gives half the remainder to daughter Krishna and 1/3 of the remainder to son Bora. Find the fraction of original land received by (a) Krishna; (b) Bora; (c) Somu herself.

time_bands.activity: Students work in small groups on Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.183 ("A tap fills 7/10 of a tank in 1 hour...."). Groups should write the multiplication expression, compute, and also respond to part (e) which requires reversing the question. After group work, one group explains part (e) to the class.

Individual work on Figure it Out Q3–Q5, section 8.1 p.183–184 ("Find the area of a rectangle with sides 3¾ ft and 9⅗ ft...."). Students must convert mixed fractions to improper fractions before multiplying. Circulate and check that students simplify using apavartana before multiplying.

Whole-class exploration of Figure it Out (product comparison), section 8.1 p.185 ("Explore when the product of two numbers is greater than both, between the two, or less than both...."). Students individually fill in the table with their own examples, then pairs compare. Lead a class discussion to articulate the three cases: both factors > 1, one or both between 0 and 1.

periods.teacher_notes: The product-comparison table in Figure it Out (product comparison), section 8.1 p.185 is conceptually the richest task in this unit — it links multiplication to the size relationships between fractions and is revisited when division is introduced. A common error is treating 'fraction × fraction always gives a smaller result'; the analysis must distinguish both factors < 1 from one factor > 1. Try This Q2, section 8.1 p.183 ("The government takes 1/6 of Somu's land....") is assigned as written homework to practise sequential fractional parts of a remainder.

periods.activity_title: What Number Cancels the Divisor? Building the Reciprocal

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (dividend-divisor-quotient), section 8.2 p.189
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore the relationship between divisor and quotient: when is the quotient greater than the dividend and when is it less? Connect to the multiplication product-comparison analysis from section 8.1.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: 6 ÷ 2 = 3 because 2 × 3 = 6. Now ask: what does 1 ÷ 2/3 mean? Which number, when multiplied by 2/3, gives 1? Write 2/3 × ? = 1 on the board and let students reason aloud. Through class discussion arrive at ? = 3/2 — the fraction with numerator and denominator swapped — and name it the reciprocal.

Apply the same reciprocal reasoning step by step to 3 ÷ 2/3, then 1/5 ÷ 1/2, then 2/3 ÷ 3/5 — the four cases the section develops. For each, write the multiplication question, identify the reciprocal, and compute. State the general rule: to divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal, giving Brahmagupta's formula a/b ÷ c/d = (a×d)/(b×c), attributed to 628 CE (and Bhāskara II's 1150 CE clarification).

Students work individually on Figure it Out (dividend-divisor-quotient), section 8.2 p.189 ("Explore the relationship between divisor and quotient: when is the quotient greater than the dividend and when is it less?...."). After individual work, hold a discussion: when the divisor is between 0 and 1 the quotient exceeds the dividend — students should connect this to the multiplication analysis established earlier in section 8.1.

periods.teacher_notes: The reasoning core of this unit is the 'multiplication question' framing: a ÷ b = ? always means b × ? = a. Students who memorise 'multiply by reciprocal' without this underpinning struggle to distinguish when to multiply and when to divide in word problems. Watch for students who swap numerator and denominator of the dividend (not the divisor) when applying the reciprocal. The dividend-divisor-quotient comparison in Figure it Out (dividend-divisor-quotient), section 8.2 p.189 cements the parallel with section 8.1's product-comparison and should not be skipped.

periods.activity_title: Dividing in Context: Tea, Bricks, and Fountains

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 8.3 p.190
textbook_items_in_class.description: Leena makes 5 cups of tea using 1/4 litre of milk. Milk per cup = 1/4 ÷ 5 = 1/4 × 1/5 = 1/20 litre.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 8.3 p.190
textbook_items_in_class.description: Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra problem: cover 7½ square units with bricks of side 1/5 unit (area 1/25 sq. units). Number of bricks = 15/2 ÷ 1/25 = 15/2 × 25 = 375/2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 8.3 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pṛithūdakasvāmī's four-fountains problem: fountains fill a cistern in 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/5 of a day respectively. Together they fill it 1+2+4+5 = 12 times a day, so the combined fill time is 1/12 day.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Example 5 blanks), section 8.3 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the four-fountains problem (Example 5): compute 1÷1/2, 1÷1/4, 1÷1/5, sum all four values, and confirm total fill time = 1/12 day.

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example 3, section 8.3 p.190 ("Leena makes 5 cups of tea using 1/4 litre of milk....") as a class, asking students to first write the division expression and then apply the reciprocal rule. Emphasise that dividing by a whole number means multiplying by its unit fraction.

Present Example 4, section 8.3 p.190 ("Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra problem: cover 7½ square units with bricks of side 1/5 unit...."). Guide students through converting 7½ to 15/2 and applying the formula; note the historical context of Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra. Students compute independently and verify by estimating: roughly 375 ÷ 2 ≈ 187 or 188 bricks, which should feel reasonable.

Present Example 5, section 8.3 p.191 ("Pṛithūdakasvāmī's four-fountains problem....") and explain the reasoning: each fountain's 'rate' is found by computing 1 ÷ (fill time). Students then complete Figure it Out (Example 5 blanks), section 8.3 p.191 ("Complete the four-fountains problem: compute 1÷1/2, 1÷1/4, 1÷1/5, sum all four values....") independently.

Class discussion: how does the four-fountains result (1/12 day) connect to the divisor-quotient relationship established in section 8.2? Students articulate that dividing by a fraction less than 1 yields a quotient greater than 1, so each fountain does more than one fill per day. Capture the generalisation on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Example 4 (Baudhāyana's brick problem) often trips students who forget to convert 7½ before dividing; pair-checking of the conversion step before applying the formula prevents this. The four-fountains problem is structurally richer than it appears: the key insight is that 'rate = 1 ÷ time', so students are dividing a fraction by a fraction without initially recognising it. The historical attributions to Pṛithūdakasvāmī (c. 860 CE) and Baudhāyana add genuine meaning — keep them brief but present.

periods.activity_title: Nested Figures, Historical Problems, and Mixed Division Practice

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 8.3 p.192
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the fraction of the whole square that the shaded region occupies in the nested figure (Fig. 8.4). The shaded part is 3/4 of a yellow triangle that is 1/2 of a red square that is 1/4 of the whole: 3/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 = 3/32.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Dramma problem), section 8.3 p.193
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the Bhāskarāchārya dramma problem: evaluate 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 1/5 × 1/16 × 1/4 of a dramma and convert to cowrie shells (1 dramma = 1280 cowrie shells). Also convert coin denominations using given rates to express 1 cowrie shell in gold dinars.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.3 p.196

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.3 p.196
homework.description: For each context, choose the correct expression and simplify: (a) Maria uses 1/4 m of lace per bag from 8 m — how many bags? (b) 1/2 m of ribbon makes 8 badges — ribbon per badge? (c) baker needs 1/6 kg flour per loaf with 5 kg available — how many loaves?

time_bands.activity: Class works through Math Talk, section 8.3 p.192 ("Find the fraction of the whole square that the shaded region occupies in the nested figure...."). Ask students to identify each nesting step before multiplying; write the chain 3/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 on the board step by step. Students then attempt Figure it Out (shaded-region diagrams), section 8.3 p.193 independently if time permits, applying the same layered-multiplication approach.

Introduce Figure it Out (Dramma problem), section 8.3 p.193 ("Complete the Bhāskarāchārya dramma problem: evaluate 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 1/5 × 1/16 × 1/4 of a dramma...."). Students compute the chain product using apavartana (cancellation) before multiplying; note that the result is 1 cowrie shell from 1 dramma. Briefly acknowledge the historical context of Bhāskarāchārya's Līlāvatī (1150 CE).

Students work individually through selected items from Figure it Out Q1, section 8.3 p.196 ("Evaluate the following divisions: 3÷4/3; 7/9÷14/4; 4/3÷3/4;...."). Encourage students to apply apavartana before computing and to verify by multiplying back. Circulate, paying attention to the item involving a mixed fraction divisor (2/3 ÷ 1⅜).

periods.teacher_notes: The nested-figure task builds directly on the unit-square area model for fraction multiplication established in section 8.1: each shading step is a multiplication, and the product of the chain gives the overall fraction. Students frequently make errors in the Dramma problem by adding fractions instead of multiplying; insist on writing each factor before computing. Figure it Out Q2, section 8.3 p.196 ("For each context, choose the correct expression....") is set for written homework to practise identifying whether a situation calls for multiplication or division.

periods.activity_title: Telescoping Products, Word Problems, and the Ant Pattern

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ant-splitting problem: a colony splits equally at each fork. Find the fraction reaching each food source for successive depths: (1−1/2); (1−1/2)(1−1/3); up to (1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/4)(1−1/5); and (1−1/2)…(1−1/10). Make a general statement and explain.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate the telescoping products: 1−1/2; (1−1/2)(1−1/3); (1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/4)(1−1/5); and (1−1/2)(1−1/3)…(1−1/10). Generalise the pattern.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mira reads a 400-page novel: she reads 1/5 of pages yesterday and 3/10 today. How many more pages remain?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mariam and cousins eat 4/5 of a cake. The remaining cake is shared equally by 3 friends. What fraction of the whole cake does each friend get?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 8.3 p.197
homework.description: Pāṭīgaṇita problem (Sridharacharya, 9th century CE): find the sum 1÷1/6 + 1÷1/10 + 1÷1/13 + 1÷1/9 + 1÷1/2.

time_bands.activity: Students compute Figure it Out Q5, section 8.3 p.197 ("Mira reads a 400-page novel: she reads 1/5 of pages yesterday and 3/10 today....") and Figure it Out Q8, section 8.3 p.197 ("Mariam and cousins eat 4/5 of a cake. The remaining cake is shared equally by 3 friends....") independently as a warm-up. These consolidate fraction multiplication and division in straightforward word contexts.

Introduce Figure it Out Q11, section 8.3 p.197 ("Ant-splitting problem: a colony splits equally at each fork...."). Students work in pairs, computing (1−1/2) first, then (1−1/2)(1−1/3), recording results in a table. Ask pairs to predict the next result before computing — encouraging pattern-guessing as the section's inductive spirit demands.

Students confirm and extend their pattern using Figure it Out Q12, section 8.3 p.197 ("Evaluate the telescoping products: 1−1/2; (1−1/2)(1−1/3);....(1−1/2)(1−1/3)…(1−1/10). Generalise the pattern."). Groups write a general statement: (1−1/2)(1−1/3)…(1−1/n) = 1/n. Ask: why does each factor 1−1/k simplify to (k−1)/k, and how do the numerators and denominators cancel telescopically?

Class shares their general statement. One or two groups explain their reasoning aloud. Close by asking students to verify the pattern holds for n = 4 and n = 5 by computing the left side. Record the generalisation on the board as the chapter's closing discovery.

periods.teacher_notes: The telescoping-product pattern is the chapter's richest generalisation and should be reached through student discovery rather than demonstration: the pair-table-predict cycle in the second band is deliberate. Students often stall on why the product simplifies so cleanly; prompting them to write out (1/2)(2/3)(3/4)… and look at which numerators and denominators cancel is usually sufficient. Figure it Out Q4, section 8.3 p.197 ("Pāṭīgaṇita problem, Sridharacharya, 9th century CE....") is set as homework to give students an independent encounter with historical division problems.

items.prompt: A factory worker completes 2/5 of a job in one hour. Which of the following correctly describes the total fraction of the job completed in 3 hours, and what is that fraction?

options.label: A
options.text: Add 3 + 2/5 because there are 3 hours; total = 17/5

options.label: B
options.text: Divide 2/5 by 3 because the job is split over hours; total = 2/15

options.label: D
options.text: Multiply 3 × 2/5 by adding 2/5 three times; total = 6/5

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option A is correct. 3 × 2/5 means adding 2/5 three times: 2/5 + 2/5 + 2/5 = 6/5. Equivalently, using the two-step procedure: divide numerator 2 by denominator 5 (conceptually), then multiply by 3 to give 6/5.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student multiplies both numerator and denominator by 3, confusing the rule for fraction × fraction with whole-number × fraction.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student adds the whole number to the fraction rather than multiplying, misreading the operation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student divides instead of multiplying, reversing the operation.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw three hops of 2/5 on a number line to see the total.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write one more real-life sentence whose answer is also 6/5, using a different context.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 8.1 p.176
exercise.description: Contextual whole-number × fraction problems: (Q1) Tenzin drinks 1/2 glass of milk daily — glasses in a week and in January; (Q2) workers make 1 km of canal in 8 days — km in 1 day and in 5-day week; (Q3) Manju and 2 neighbours share 5 litres of oil among 3 families — oil per family per week and in 4 weeks; (Q4) Moon sets 5/6 hour later each day — hours after 10 pm on Thursday.

items.prompt: Using the unit-square area model, what is the product 1/3 × 1/4?

options.label: A
options.text: 1/12, because the unit square is divided into 3 columns and 4 rows giving 12 equal parts, and 1 part is shaded.

options.label: B
options.text: 1/7, because 3 + 4 = 7 and the product shares their sum as the denominator.

options.label: C
options.text: 2/7, because the numerators add and the denominators add.

options.label: D
options.text: 4/3, because you divide the larger denominator by the smaller.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1/12. Dividing the unit square into 3 equal columns and 4 equal rows creates 12 equal cells; the cell at the intersection of the first column and first row is 1/12 of the whole.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student adds the denominators instead of multiplying them, a classic fraction-addition error applied to multiplication.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student adds both numerators and both denominators, showing confusion between addition and multiplication of fractions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student divides denominators, inverting the operation and ignoring the area model's structure.

inclusivity.support: Have the student draw the unit square on squared paper, shade one column and one row, and count the small squares.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain, in their own words, why the denominator of the product is always the product of the two denominators.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.180
exercise.description: Find the following products using a unit square as the whole: (a) 1/3 × 1/5; (b) 1/4 × 1/3; (c) 1/5 × 1/2; (d) 1/6 × 1/5. Then find 1/12 × 1/18 without drawing.

items.prompt: Ravi says: 'When I divide a number by a fraction that is less than 1, the answer is always smaller than the number I started with.' Is Ravi correct? Justify your answer using the reciprocal reasoning developed in section 8.2, and support your explanation with one numerical example.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ravi is incorrect. When you divide by a fraction between 0 and 1, the quotient is greater than the dividend, not smaller. Using the reciprocal reasoning: a ÷ (c/d) means finding a number that, when multiplied by c/d, gives a. Since c/d < 1, its reciprocal d/c > 1, so multiplying a by d/c gives a result larger than a. Example: 3 ÷ (1/2) = 3 × 2 = 6, and 6 > 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Frame a ÷ (c/d) as 'c/d × ? = a', identify ? = a × d/c; since d/c > 1 when c/d < 1, the quotient exceeds the dividend.

inclusivity.support: Let the student talk through the argument with a partner before writing, using the specific example 1 ÷ (1/2).
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: what happens if the divisor equals exactly 1? What if it is exactly 1/2 versus exactly 2? Alter one value and re-explain the direction of the inequality.

exercise.description: Explore the relationship between divisor and quotient: when is the quotient greater than the dividend and when is it less? Connect to the multiplication product-comparison analysis from section 8.1.

items.prompt: A storage tank is filled to 3/4 of its capacity. A pump transfers 2/3 of the water currently in the tank to a second container. What fraction of the full tank's capacity is now in the second container? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The second container receives 2/3 of the water in the first tank. Water in the first tank = 3/4 of full capacity. So the fraction transferred = 2/3 × 3/4 = (2×3)/(3×4) = 6/12 = 1/2. The second container holds 1/2 of the full tank's capacity.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply a/b × c/d = (a×c)/(b×d): 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2; cancel the factor of 3 before multiplying.

inclusivity.support: Draw the unit square: shade 3 out of 4 columns for the tank's water, then shade 2 out of 3 rows within the shaded region and count the cells.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the pump to transfer only 5/6 of the water and re-solve; then state whether the second container is more or less than half full, explaining why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.183
exercise.description: A tap fills 7/10 of a tank in 1 hour. Find the fraction filled if the tap runs for: (a) 1/3 hour; (b) 2/3 hour; (c) 3/4 hour; (d) 7/10 hour; (e) how long must the tap run to fill the tank completely?

items.prompt: A cook has 3/4 litre of soup and wants to fill small bowls that each hold 3/8 litre. How many bowls can be completely filled? Show your working using the reciprocal method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Number of bowls = 3/4 ÷ 3/8. Multiply by the reciprocal of 3/8, which is 8/3: 3/4 × 8/3 = (3×8)/(4×3) = 24/12 = 2. Exactly 2 bowls can be completely filled.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line marked in eighths from 0 to 3/4 and count how many 3/8 segments fit.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the bowl size to 5/12 litre and re-solve; decide whether the answer is a whole number and explain what the remainder means in context.

exercise.description: Leena makes 5 cups of tea using 1/4 litre of milk. Milk per cup = 1/4 ÷ 5 = 1/4 × 1/5 = 1/20 litre.

items.prompt: A large square is divided into four equal smaller squares. One of those smaller squares is divided into four equal parts, and one of those parts is shaded. What fraction of the original large square is shaded? Show each multiplication step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: each smaller square is 1/4 of the large square. Step 2: one part of the four-equal division of that smaller square is 1/4 of that smaller square. Shaded fraction = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 of the large square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply successive multiplication: shaded = (1/4 of the large square) × (1/4 of that piece) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

inclusivity.support: Draw the large square, divide it into four equal parts, then divide one part into four more, and shade one tiny cell — count cells to verify.
inclusivity.challenge: Add a third layer: divide the shaded 1/16 piece into four equal parts and shade three of them. What fraction of the original square is now shaded?

exercise.description: Find the fraction of the whole square that the shaded region occupies in the nested figure (Fig. 8.4). The shaded part is 3/4 of a yellow triangle that is 1/2 of a red square that is 1/4 of the whole: 3/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 = 3/32.

items.prompt: Compute the product (1 − 1/2) × (1 − 1/3) × (1 − 1/4). Write each factor as a fraction, multiply step by step using cancellation, and state what pattern you notice about the result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (1 − 1/2) = 1/2; (1 − 1/3) = 2/3; (1 − 1/4) = 3/4. Product = 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4. Cancel: the 2 in the numerator of 2/3 cancels with the 2 in the denominator of 1/2; the 3 in the numerator of 3/4 cancels with the 3 in the denominator of 2/3. Result = 1/4. The pattern: (1−1/2)(1−1/3)…(1−1/n) = 1/n; here n = 4, giving 1/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write each factor as (k−1)/k, multiply and cancel telescopically: numerators and denominators cancel leaving 1/n.

inclusivity.support: Use a number line or diagram to show the product shrinking at each step: mark 1/2, then 1/3 of 1/2, then 1/4 of the result.
inclusivity.challenge: Extend the product to n = 6 and verify the result equals 1/6; then write a one-sentence general rule using algebra.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 8.3 p.197
exercise.description: Ant-splitting problem: a colony splits equally at each fork. Find the fraction reaching each food source for successive depths: (1−1/2); (1−1/2)(1−1/3); up to (1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/4)(1−1/5); and (1−1/2)…(1−1/10). Make a general statement and explain.
